name: Bilal Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bilal, I'm 27, and I'm a junior lawyer at Carter and Pryce, a small firm above a phone shop on the high street. I do housing work, mostly tenants facing eviction, a lot of it paid by legal aid, which is the government scheme that pays for lawyers for people who can't afford one. I live with my partner Inès, who's a nurse on nights at the general hospital, so we mostly see each other at breakfast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in at half eight and the first thing is the duty phone, people ringing because a bailiff's letter came. Then it's drafting defences, chasing landlords for repair records, and filling in legal aid forms, which honestly take a third of my week. I like the clients, even the angry ones, because when you save someone's flat they remember your name. What wears me out is the paperwork and knowing I'm still slower than the others at spotting the point that wins a case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the tech was never the problem, the funding was. Legal aid rates haven't gone up in years and that's why firms like ours are hanging on by a thread. If AI only shaves a bit off the forms, fine, but it doesn't fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as tight as it is now, which isn't great. We've got about three weeks of money in the bank and my student loan comes out every month. Carter and Pryce lost two legal aid contracts last year, so I already wonder if my job outlasts the next round of cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the housing work and use the research tool the firm pays for a bit more, since it does save me an hour on case summaries. I'd also join the legal aid lawyers' association properly, not just read their emails. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, even if that means fewer takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, mostly. It's not scary in a new way, it's the same old worry. Every month I check the bank on the day before payday and do the maths in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm lost two contracts. What would happen if it lost another one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Mr Pryce would have to let someone go, and I'm the newest and the slowest, so I know who it'd be. There's one other firm doing housing work in this town and it's not hiring. I'd probably have to commute an hour each way to the city, which with Inès on nights means we'd barely see each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inès if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight, because she'd see it on my face anyway. She'd say we'll manage, because she always does. If the firm cut me, Inès (his partner) would pick up extra night shifts to cover us, and I'd hate that more than losing the job.

say: The real problem for **legal aid** firms is **funding**, not technology.
AI saving an hour on forms doesn't fix a **broken system** for tenants.
think: My life stays **tight**: about **three weeks** of savings and a student loan.
As the **newest and slowest** junior, I'd be the first cut if the firm shrinks.
do: Use the firm's **research tool** more to save an hour on case summaries.
Join the **legal aid lawyers' association** properly this year.
Put **fifty a month** aside by cutting back on takeaways.
feel: **Flat** rather than scared, because this is the **same old worry** about money.
S0.quote: If the firm cut me, Inès (his partner) would pick up extra night shifts to cover us, and I'd hate that more than losing the job.
fieldNote: His **money worry** comes before AI: the firm has already lost **two contracts**.
He blames **funding policy**, not technology, and puts his energy into a lawyers' association.
The sharpest feeling was **guilt** about Inès working more nights to cover him.

steps.text: Use the firm's research tool for case summaries to save an hour
Join the legal aid lawyers' association and go to its meetings
Put fifty a month aside by cutting takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, if it clears the forms, but who's checking the machine when it gets a tenant's case wrong? I'd be posting about how the people we help can't afford to be a test case. Regulation first, then roll it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know a lot of what I do is exactly the stuff on that list: writing, checking, filling in. A machine could draft my defences faster than me, and I'm not the best at it yet. So I think Carter and Pryce would keep the two seniors and maybe one junior who's good with the tools, and that might not be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop avoiding the tools and get properly good at the firm's drafting software in the first few months, since others have already shown it works. I'd also look at the jobs that need a person in a room, like being the duty lawyer at the county court on possession days. And I'd talk to the association about pushing for rules on AI in legal aid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit sick. I spent four years and a lot of borrowed money learning to do the thing the card says machines take over. At the same time, part of me thinks if it's proven, I should just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop avoiding the tools. What's held you back so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I'm still learning the law itself, and I didn't want a shortcut that hides what I don't know. Zoe (the other junior) uses it all the time and her drafts come back cleaner than mine. That stings a bit, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the court work look like, and why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On possession days there's a list of thirty tenants and a duty lawyer runs between them in the corridor. You've got ten minutes to read a file and talk a frightened person down before they go in. A machine can read the file, but somebody still has to stand in that court corridor and calm a frightened tenant down.

say: I'd welcome AI clearing **forms**, but insist on **regulation** before it touches tenants' cases.
People on **legal aid** shouldn't be the test cases for new software.
think: Most of my day is **writing and checking**, exactly what the card says AI takes over.
The firm may keep one **tool-savvy junior**, and that might be Zoe rather than me.
do: Get properly good at the firm's **drafting software** within a few months.
Push for **duty lawyer** shifts at the county court on possession days.
Lobby through the association for **rules on AI** in legal aid work.
feel: **Sick** about four years of borrowed money spent on skills machines now take over.
Also a **steady** sense that he should just get on with it once it's proven.
S1.quote: A machine can read the file, but somebody still has to stand in that court corridor and calm a frightened tenant down.
fieldNote: He openly compares himself to **Zoe**, the other junior, and expects to lose that race.
His escape route is the **court corridor**, the one part of the job that needs a body.
Publicly he leads with **regulation**; privately he's mostly worried about his own place.

steps.text: Learn the firm's drafting software in the first three months
Ask Mr Pryce for duty lawyer shifts at the county court
Lobby through the association for AI rules in legal aid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to step in, with income support and real protection for workers. Nobody voted for this. I'd be in every union meeting going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as a lawyer before I've really started. If a machine can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then drafting a defence or reading a tenancy is the first to go. Two years isn't enough time to become senior enough to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop paying extra on anything and move every spare pound into savings, even if it's only a few hundred. I'd look hard at work that needs hands, because the robots come three years after, around 2031. My uncle Karim runs a small removals firm and he's always short of people, so I'd ask him for weekend work straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. It's like being told the house you're halfway through building is being knocked down. And I'm cross, because the people who built this will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said removals. How would that sit with you, after law school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd hurt my pride, but carrying sofas pays rent and I'm not too proud for rent. And it buys me three years while robots catch up. I'd rather be lifting boxes for Karim (his uncle) than sitting at home refreshing job sites that don't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your tenants? Who helps them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what really keeps me up. If AI handles their cases for free, maybe they're better off, I genuinely don't know. But if it's a landlord's AI against a tenant with nothing, that's not justice, that's just a faster eviction.

say: Governments must bring in **income support** and worker protection **immediately**.
Nobody voted for this, and I'd be at **every union meeting**.
think: I'm **finished as a lawyer** before I've properly started.
**Two years** is far too short to become senior enough to matter.
do: Stop extra spending and move every spare pound into **savings** right away.
Ask uncle Karim for **weekend removals** work to buy three years before robots.
Go to **union meetings** pushing for income support.
feel: **Scared**, like a half-built house being **knocked down**.
**Angry** that the people who built this will be fine.
S2.quote: If it's a landlord's AI against a tenant with nothing, that's not justice, that's just a faster eviction.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year robot gap** clearly and would use it for hands-on work.
Turning to his uncle's **removals firm** is about rent, not choice, and it costs him pride.
Even at his most scared he talks about **tenants**, not just himself.

steps.text: Move every spare pound into savings from the first month
Ask uncle Karim for weekend shifts at his removals firm
Go to union meetings pushing for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder, because five years means there's no excuse for being unprepared. I'd be saying the government has five years to plan, so where's the plan? Retraining money, a proper safety net, that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it buys me a bit more time as a lawyer, maybe till 2030, but the end is the same. By then I'd be a few years qualified, which helps a little, but not against something that does the whole job. I'd still be the one who isn't quite good enough to be the last person they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Carter and Pryce for two or three years and save as hard as I can, maybe a hundred a month now. Meanwhile I'd look at training as a tenancy relations officer at the council, a job that's half visiting homes and half talking to landlords. And I'd join the association's campaign on AI in courts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days and alarmed on the bad ones. Five years sounds long until you count it in rent payments. Sixty rent payments, that's how I'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the council job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you're out in people's flats, looking at damp and broken boilers and talking a landlord round on the doorstep. It uses what I know about housing law, but it's mostly being there. The robots for that kind of thing would come later, around 2034, so it gives me a bit more road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Inès change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids in a few years, and I think we'd wait longer. Inès's job is safer than mine because nursing is hands-on, so we'd lean on her wage. I'd feel like a passenger for a while, and I don't love that.

say: The government gets **five years** of warning, so it has **no excuse** not to plan.
We need **retraining money** and a proper safety net, starting now.
think: Maybe I last as a lawyer **until 2030**, but the end is the same.
I'd still be the one who isn't quite **good enough** to be kept last.
do: Stay at the firm for two or three years, saving a **hundred a month**.
Train for a **tenancy relations officer** role at the council.
Join the association's campaign on **AI in courts**.
feel: **Uneasy** most days and alarmed on bad ones.
He counts the time as **sixty rent payments**, not five years.
S3.quote: Five years sounds long until you count it in rent payments. Sixty rent payments, that's how I'd think about it.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the legal job**, so extra time doesn't lower the stakes.
His plan uses housing law in a more **hands-on council** role with later robot risk.
He'd **delay children** and lean on Inès's safer nursing wage, which bothers him.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month while staying at Carter and Pryce
Apply for council training as a tenancy relations officer
Join the association's campaign on AI in courts
Put off having children with Inès for a few more years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a real chance, and if we waste it that's a political choice. I'd want legal aid to fund lawyers who check AI decisions for tenants. That's a job that could exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think ten years is enough to make a proper move without panicking. I'd be 37, which is young enough to start something new. I still think the lawyer job as I know it ends, but I'm less frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in housing law for five or six years and get properly competent, using the AI tools daily once they're proven. Around year five I'd start the council housing inspector qualification at evening classes. And I'd keep putting money aside, and keep going to the association, because rules get made in that decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a knot, but I can breathe. Ten years feels like time to do things on purpose rather than in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned three different plans across the pictures. Which one is really you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council one, I think. Removals was me panicking and staying put was me pretending. Housing inspection uses what I care about and keeps me in people's homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a first-year law student who asked you for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the law, but learn people harder. The bit of the job a machine won't do for a while is sitting with someone at their kitchen table. Everything else, assume it's going.

Legal aid should fund lawyers who **check AI decisions** for tenants.
think: **Ten years** is enough for a proper career move without panicking.
The lawyer job **as I know it** still ends, but I'm less frightened.

S4.quote: Learn the law, but learn people harder. The bit of the job a machine won't do for a while is sitting with someone at their kitchen table.
fieldNote: He named the **council housing** route as his real plan and called the others panic.
He is **steady** with technology: daily AI use once it's **proven**, not before.
Still anxious because he expects the **legal job** to end, just more slowly.

steps.text: Use AI drafting tools daily at Carter and Pryce once proven
Start the council housing inspector course at evening classes
Keep up monthly savings while still a junior lawyer
Stay active in the legal aid lawyers' association

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years is no time when you've got three weeks of savings and a job a machine can do. What would help is income support while people retrain, and legal aid money for humans who check what the machines decide for tenants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the clients more. Everyone asks what happens to lawyers. Nobody asks what happens to the woman with two kids and a damp flat when the only thing between her and the landlord is an app.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks what happens to the woman with two kids and a damp flat when the only thing between her and the landlord is an app.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** junior housing lawyer at a small **legal aid** firm on a town high street.
He lives with Inès, a night-shift **nurse**, on about **three weeks** of savings and a student loan.
He blames **funding cuts** more than technology and turns to his lawyers' association for answers.
In fast AGI he'd take **removals work** from his uncle; with more time he'd retrain for **council housing** work.
Across every picture he keeps returning to the **tenants** who'd face a landlord's AI alone.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years and thin savings leave no room to move.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while people retrain, so he isn't forced into any job going.
**Legal aid funding** for human lawyers who check AI decisions for tenants.
